chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter XVIII
paragraphs: It was a long time before Pierre could fall asleep that night. He paced up and down his room, now frowning over a difficult problem, now suddenly shrugging his shoulders and wincing, now smiling happily.

He was thinking about Prince Andrew, about Natasha, about their love—one moment jealous of her past, the next reproaching himself for that feeling. It was already six in the morning and he still paced the room.

"Well, what's to be done if there's no way around it? What can I do? Obviously this is how it has to be," he told himself, and hastily undressing, he got into bed—happy and agitated, but free of hesitation or indecision.
"Strange and impossible as such happiness seems, I must do everything I can so that she and I may become husband and wife," he told himself.
A few days earlier Pierre had decided to leave for Petersburg on Friday. When he woke on Thursday, Savelich came to ask about packing for the trip.

"What—Petersburg? What is Petersburg? Who's in Petersburg?" he asked, though only of himself. "Oh yes, a long time ago—before all this happened—I did mean to go to Petersburg for some reason," he reflected. "Why? But maybe I will go... What a good, considerate fellow he is!" he thought, looking at Savelich. "And what a nice smile!"
"Well, Savelich, do you still not want to accept your freedom?" Pierre asked him.
"What good is freedom to me, your excellency? We lived under the late count—God rest his soul!—and we've lived under you too, and never been mistreated."
"And your children?"
"The children will be fine just the same. With masters like you, anyone can get along."
"But what about my heirs?" said Pierre. "Suppose I suddenly get married... it could happen," he added with an involuntary smile.
"If I may say so, your excellency, that would be a very good thing."
"He thinks it's so easy," Pierre thought. "He doesn't know how terrifying it is, how dangerous. Too soon or too late... it's terrifying!"
"So what are your orders? Are you leaving tomorrow?" asked Savelich.

"No, I'll put it off a bit. I'll tell you later. Forgive me for the trouble I've put you through," said Pierre, and seeing Savelich smile, he thought: "How strange it is that he doesn't know there is no Petersburg for me now, and that this has to be settled first. But he probably does know and is just pretending. Should I talk to him about it? No, some other time."
At breakfast, Pierre told the princess—his cousin—that he'd been to see Princess Mary the day before and had met there—"Guess who? Natasha Rostova!"
The princess seemed to find this no more remarkable than if he'd seen some Anna Semyonovna.
"Do you know her?" Pierre asked.
"I've seen the princess," she replied. "I heard they were arranging a match for her with young Rostov. That would be very good for the Rostovs—they're said to be completely ruined."
"No—I mean, do you know Natasha Rostova?"
"I heard about that business of hers at the time. It was very unfortunate."
"She either doesn't understand or she's pretending," Pierre thought. "Better not say anything to her either."
The princess had also prepared provisions for Pierre's journey.
"How kind they all are," Pierre thought. "What's amazing is that they bother with these things now, when none of it could matter to them anymore. And all for me!"
That same day the Chief of Police came to Pierre, inviting him to send a representative to the Faceted Palace to collect property that was being returned to its owners.

"And this man too," thought Pierre, studying the Chief of Police's face. "What a fine, good-looking officer, and how kind. Think of him bothering with such trifles right now! And people actually say he's dishonest and takes bribes. What nonsense! And besides, why shouldn't he take bribes? That's how he was raised. Everyone does it. But what a pleasant, kind face, and how he smiles as he looks at me!"
Pierre went to Princess Mary's for dinner.

As he drove through the streets past burned-out houses, he was struck by the beauty of those ruins. The chimney stacks and crumbling walls, stretching out to conceal one another, reminded him of the Rhine and the Colosseum. The cab drivers and passengers he passed, the carpenters working on frames for new buildings, the women selling goods at the street corners—all looked at him with cheerful, beaming faces that seemed to say: "Ah, here he is! Let's see what comes of this!"

At the entrance to Princess Mary's house, Pierre felt unsure whether he had really been there the night before, really seen Natasha and talked with her. "Maybe I imagined it. Maybe I'll go in and find no one." But he had barely entered the room when he felt her presence—felt it through the sudden loss of his freedom. She was wearing the same black dress with soft folds, and her hair was arranged the same way as the evening before, but she was completely different. If she had looked like this the night before when he entered the room, he couldn't have failed to recognize her for a single instant.
She was as he had known her almost as a child and later as Prince Andrew's fiancée. A bright, questioning light shone in her eyes, and her face wore a friendly and strangely playful expression.
Pierre stayed for dinner and would have spent the whole evening there, but Princess Mary was going to vespers and Pierre left with her.

The next day he came early, stayed for dinner, and spent the whole evening. Though Princess Mary and Natasha were clearly glad to see their visitor, and though all of Pierre's interest was now centered on that house, by evening they had talked over everything and the conversation kept moving between those insignificant topics that arise when people want to keep talking but can't find new subjects. Pierre stayed so late that Princess Mary and Natasha kept exchanging glances, obviously waiting for him to leave. Pierre saw this but couldn't bring himself to go. He felt heavy and awkward, but still sat on because he simply couldn't get up and leave.
Princess Mary, foreseeing no end to it, was the first to rise and, complaining of a headache, began to say good night.
"So you're going to Petersburg tomorrow?" she asked.

"No, I'm not going," Pierre replied hastily, in a surprised, almost offended tone. "Yes... no... to Petersburg? Tomorrow—but I won't say goodbye yet. I'll come by in case you have any errands for me," he said, standing before Princess Mary, flushing and fidgeting, not leaving.

Natasha gave him her hand and left the room. Princess Mary, instead of going, sank into an armchair and fixed her deep, radiant eyes on him with a look that was both stern and intent. The weariness she'd plainly shown before had completely vanished. With a deep, heavy sigh she seemed to be preparing herself for a long conversation.
The instant Natasha left, Pierre's awkwardness and confusion disappeared and were replaced by eager excitement. He quickly pulled a chair up to Princess Mary.

"Yes, I wanted to tell you," he said, responding to her look as if she had spoken. "Princess, help me! What should I do? Can I hope? Princess, my dear friend, listen! I know everything. I know I'm not worthy of her, I know it's impossible to talk about it now. But I want to be her brother. No, I don't... I can't..."
He paused and rubbed his face and eyes with his hands.

"Well," he went on, clearly struggling for self-control and coherence. "I don't know when I first began to love her, but I've loved her and her alone all my life, and I love her so much that I can't imagine life without her. I can't ask for her hand right now, but the thought that maybe she could be mine, and that I might miss that chance... that chance... is terrible. Tell me—can I hope? Tell me, what should I do? Dear princess!" he said after a brief pause, touching her hand when she didn't reply.
"I'm thinking about what you've told me," Princess Mary answered. "This is what I'll say. You're right that to speak to her of love at present—"

Princess Mary stopped. She'd been about to say that speaking of love was impossible, but she stopped because she had seen from the sudden change in Natasha two days ago that Natasha would not only not be hurt if Pierre spoke of his love, but that it was the one thing she wanted.
"To speak to her now wouldn't do," the princess said all the same.
"But what am I to do?"
"Leave it to me," said Princess Mary. "I know..."
Pierre was looking into Princess Mary's eyes.
"Well?... Well?..." he said.
"I know that she loves... will love you," Princess Mary corrected herself.
Before the words were out, Pierre had sprung up and seized Princess Mary's hand with a frightened expression.
"What makes you think so? You think I can hope? You think—?"
"Yes, I think so," said Princess Mary with a smile. "Write to her parents, and leave it to me. I'll tell her when the time is right. I want this to happen, and my heart tells me it will."
"No, it can't be! How happy I am! But it can't be... How happy I am! No, it can't be!" Pierre kept saying as he kissed Princess Mary's hands.
"Go to Petersburg—that would be best. And I'll write to you," she said.
"To Petersburg? Go there? Very well, I'll go. But may I come again tomorrow?"

The next day Pierre came to say goodbye. Natasha was less animated than the day before; but as he looked at her, Pierre sometimes felt as if he were vanishing, as if neither he nor she existed anymore, that nothing existed but happiness. "Can this be real? No, it can't," he told himself at every glance, every gesture, every word that filled his heart with joy.
When, saying goodbye, he took her thin, slender hand, he couldn't help holding it a little longer in his.

"Is it possible that this hand, this face, those eyes—all this treasure of feminine charm, so strange to me now—is it possible that one day it will be mine forever, as familiar as I am to myself?... No, that's impossible!"
"Goodbye, Count," she said aloud. "I'll very much look forward to your return," she added in a whisper.

And these simple words, her look, and the expression on her face that accompanied them formed, for two months, the subject of inexhaustible memories, interpretations, and happy meditations for Pierre. "'I'll very much look forward to your return.' How did she say it? How did she look? What did she mean? What was the look in her eyes?" And his recalled impression was so vivid that it seemed to happen right then, and he would smile all over again.

chapters.title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter XIX
paragraphs: There was nothing in Pierre's soul now that resembled what had troubled him during his courtship of Helene.

He did not repeat to himself with a sickening feeling of shame the words he had spoken, or think: "Oh, why didn't I say that?" and "Whatever made me say 'I love you'?" On the contrary, he now replayed in his mind every word he or Natasha had said, down to the smallest detail of her face and smile, and wanted to add nothing and take nothing away. He only wished he could say it all again. "Was it right when she said, 'Leave it to me'? Did she really see into my soul? Yes, she did," Pierre told himself. "And she's wonderful! 'Something fine!'—how she said it! And her eyes. And how she blushed when she said: 'I'll very much look forward to your return'... She loves me. Yes, she loves me." That was the only worry that often troubled Pierre. He made no plans now. The happiness before him seemed so inconceivable that if only he could reach it, there would be nothing beyond. Everything ended there.

That was the only doubt that often troubled Pierre. He made no plans now. The happiness before him seemed so inconceivable that if only he could reach it, it would be the end of everything. Nothing would come after.

A joyful, unexpected frenzy—which he had thought himself incapable of—possessed him. The whole meaning of life, not for him alone but for the whole world, seemed to him centered in his love and the possibility of being loved by her. At times everyone seemed to him to be occupied with one thing only—his future happiness. Sometimes it seemed to him that everyone was as happy as he was, and merely tried to hide that happiness by pretending to be busy with other things. In every word and gesture he saw hints of his own happiness. He often startled people who met him by his meaningful, joyful looks and smiles, which seemed to express a secret understanding between them. But when he realized that people might not know about his happiness, he pitied them with all his heart and felt the urge to somehow explain to them that everything they were occupied with was absolute nonsense and trivialities not worth thinking about.

When people suggested he enter the civil service, or when the war or general political affairs were discussed on the assumption that everyone's well-being depended on some particular turn of events, he would listen with his mild, compassionate smile, and startle everyone with his strange comments. But those who thought they understood Pierre, as well as those who didn't, all felt at this time that he was a delightful and extraordinary person—generous, gentle, clever, cheerful, and magnanimous.

When dealing with the affairs and papers of his dead wife, her memory stirred in him nothing but pity that she had never known the joy he now knew. Prince Vasili, who had gotten a new post and some fresh decorations and was especially proud of himself just then, struck Pierre as a touching, kind, and pitiable old man.

Often in later life Pierre recalled this period of blissful madness. All the views he formed of people and situations during this time remained true for him always. He not only never renounced them later, but when he was in doubt or felt conflicted, he would ask himself what he would have thought at that time, and that perspective never failed him.

"I may have seemed strange and eccentric then," he thought, "but I wasn't as crazy as it looked. On the contrary, I was wiser and had more insight then than at any other time, and I understood everything worth understanding in life, because... because I was happy."

Pierre's madness consisted in this: he no longer waited, as he once did, to discover personal qualities—what he called "good qualities"—in people before loving them. His heart was now overflowing with love, and by loving people without cause, he discovered undeniable reasons to love them.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter XX
paragraphs: After Pierre's departure that first evening, when Natasha had said to Princess Mary with a mischievous, mocking smile: "He looks just—yes, just as if he'd come out of a Russian bath, in a short coat and with his hair cropped"—from that moment something hidden and unknown to her but irresistible awoke in Natasha's soul.

Everything about her—her face, her walk, her look, her voice—was suddenly changed. To her own surprise, a force of life and a hope of happiness rose to the surface and demanded to be satisfied. From that evening she seemed to have forgotten everything that had happened to her. She never again complained about her situation, never said a word about the past, and was no longer afraid to make cheerful plans for the future. She spoke little of Pierre, but when Princess Mary mentioned him, a long-extinguished light flickered in her eyes and her lips curved in a strange smile.

The change that took place in Natasha at first surprised Princess Mary, but when she understood what it meant, it grieved her. "Can she have loved my brother so little that she could forget him so quickly?" she thought when she reflected on the change. But when she was with Natasha, she wasn't angry with her and didn't reproach her. The awakened force of life that had taken hold of Natasha was clearly so powerful and beyond her control that Princess Mary felt she had no right to reproach her, even in her own heart.
Natasha gave herself up so fully and openly to this new feeling that she didn't even try to hide the fact that she was no longer sad but bright and cheerful.
When Princess Mary returned to her room after her late-night conversation with Pierre, Natasha met her at the door.
"He's spoken? Yes? He has spoken?" she repeated.
And a joyful yet pitiful expression—which seemed to beg forgiveness for her joy—settled on Natasha's face.
"I wanted to listen at the door, but I knew you'd tell me."
However touching the look Natasha gave her seemed to Princess Mary, and however sorry she felt seeing her excitement, these words pained her for a moment. She remembered her brother and his love.
"But what can be done? She can't help it," the princess thought.
And with a sad, somewhat stern expression she told Natasha everything Pierre had said. Hearing that he was going to Petersburg, Natasha was stunned.
"To Petersburg!" she repeated, as if unable to understand.
But noticing the grieved look on Princess Mary's face, she guessed the reason for that sadness and suddenly began to cry.
"Mary," she said, "tell me what I should do! I'm afraid of being bad. Whatever you tell me, I'll do. Tell me..."
"You love him?"
"Yes," Natasha whispered.
"Then why are you crying? I'm happy for you," said Princess Mary, who—because of those tears—had already quite forgiven Natasha's joy.
"It won't be right away—someday. Just think how wonderful it will be when I'm his wife and you marry Nicholas!"
"Natasha, I've asked you not to talk about that. Let's talk about you."
They were silent for a while.
"But why go to Petersburg?" Natasha suddenly asked, and quickly answered her own question. "No, no—he has to... Yes, Mary, he has to."

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter I
paragraphs: Seven years had passed. The storm-tossed sea of European history had subsided within its shores and seemed to have grown calm. But the mysterious forces that move humanity—mysterious because the laws governing them are unknown to us—continued to operate.

Though the surface of the sea of history appeared motionless, the movement of humanity went on as ceaselessly as the flow of time. Various groups of people formed and dissolved, the formation and dissolution of kingdoms and displacements of peoples were in preparation.

The sea of history was no longer driven violently from shore to shore as before. It was churning in its depths. Historical figures were no longer carried by the waves from one shore to another. They now seemed to spin in place. Historical figures who had formerly commanded armies and directed the movement of masses through wars, campaigns, and battles now guided the surging masses through political and diplomatic maneuvers, laws, and treaties.
Historians call this activity of historical figures "the reaction."

In describing this period, they sternly condemn the historical figures who, in their view, caused what they call the reaction. All the prominent people of that era—from Alexander and Napoleon to Madame de Stael, Photius, Schelling, Fichte, Chateaubriand, and others—are arraigned before their stern tribunal and acquitted or condemned according to whether they promoted progress or reaction.

According to these accounts, a reaction took place in Russia too at this time, and the chief culprit was Alexander I—the same man who, according to these same historians, was the chief cause of the liberal reforms at the start of his reign, the savior of Russia, and the hero of Europe. Yet in present-day Russian literature, from schoolboy essayists to serious historians, there is no one who does not criticize Alexander for the things he supposedly did wrong during this period.
There is no one in Russian literature now, from schoolboy essayists to learned historians, who does not take a shot at Alexander for his mistakes during this phase of his reign.

"He should have acted this way, not that way. In this case he did well; in that case, badly. He was admirable at the start of his reign and during 1812, but was wrong to give a constitution to Poland, create the Holy Alliance, empower Arakcheyev, encourage Golitsyn and mysticism, and then encourage Shishkov and Photius. He was wrong to interfere with the army's front-line administration; he was wrong to disband the Semyonovsky regiment, and so on and so on."
It would take a dozen pages to list all the criticisms historians make of him, based on their knowledge of what is good for humanity.
What do these criticisms mean?

Don't the very actions for which historians praise Alexander I—the liberal reforms at the start of his reign, the struggle with Napoleon, the firmness he showed in 1812, and the campaign of 1813—flow from the same sources, the same conditions of birth, education, and life that shaped Alexander's personality and produced the actions for which historians blame him, such as the Holy Alliance, the restoration of Poland, and the reaction of the 1820s?
What is the real substance of these criticisms?

It lies in the fact that a historical figure like Alexander I, standing at the highest possible pinnacle of human power, in the blinding light of history focused upon him—exposed to the strongest influences imaginable: the intrigues, flattery, and self-deception inseparable from power, and feeling a responsibility for everything happening in Europe at every moment of his life—proved to be, not fifty years ago but today, not a person of particularly virtuous character. That is what the historians' criticisms amount to.

But even if we assume that Alexander was mistaken fifty years ago in his idea of what was good for the people, we must also assume that the historian who judges him will, after some time, also turn out to be wrong in his understanding of what is good for humanity. This assumption is all the more natural and inevitable because the development of history shows us that every year, with every new writer, what we consider good for humanity changes. What once seemed good—giving Poland a constitution and forming the Holy Alliance—is later regarded as harmful. What seems harmful—the Napoleonic wars, the spread of revolutionary ideas—is later recognized as good.

Alexander's activity, or Napoleon's, cannot be called useful or harmful, because we cannot say what it was useful or harmful for. If someone dislikes it, that is only because it doesn't match their limited understanding of what is good. Whether I see the preservation of my father's house in Moscow in 1812 as good, or the glory of the Russian army, or the prosperity of Petersburg's university or Poland's freedom, or Russia's greatness, or Europe's balance of power, or a certain kind of European civilization called "progress"—I must acknowledge that the activity of any historical figure had, besides these aims, other aims more broadly and universally human that are beyond my grasp.

But let us suppose that what is called science can reconcile all contradictions and possesses an unchanging standard of good and bad by which to judge historical characters and events; let us say that Alexander could have done everything differently; let us even say that—guided by those who criticize him, who claim to know the ultimate goal of humanity's movement—he could have followed the program of nationalism, freedom, equality, and progress (for there seems to be no other) that his present-day critics would prescribe for him. Let us assume all that was possible. What then would have become of the activity of all the people who opposed the direction that the government was taking at that time? Their activity would not have existed; there would have been no life; there would have been nothing.
If we accept that human life can be governed by reason, then the very possibility of life is destroyed.

chapters.title: First Epilogue (1813 - 20) — Chapter II
paragraphs: If we assume, as historians do, that great men lead humanity toward the attainment of certain goals—the greatness of Russia or of France, the balance of power in Europe, the spread of revolutionary ideas, general progress, or anything else—then it is impossible to explain the facts of history without resorting to the concepts of "chance" and "genius."

If the goal of the European wars at the start of the nineteenth century had been the expansion of Russia, that goal could have been achieved without all the preceding wars and without the invasion. If the goal had been the expansion of France, that goal could have been reached without the Revolution and without the Empire. If the goal had been the spread of ideas, the printing press would have accomplished that far better than soldiers. If the goal had been the progress of civilization, one can easily imagine that there were other paths to spreading civilization besides the destruction of people and their wealth.
Why did it happen this way and not some other?
Because it just happened that way! "Chance created the situation; genius made use of it," says history.
But what is chance? What is genius?

The words "chance" and "genius" do not refer to anything that actually exists, and therefore cannot be defined. They only indicate a certain stage in our understanding of events. I don't know why a certain event occurs; I think I cannot know; so I don't try to know, and I say: "chance." I see a force producing effects beyond the scope of ordinary human powers; I don't understand why this happens, and I say: "genius."

To a flock of sheep, the ram that the shepherd drives each evening into a special pen to be fattened—growing twice as fat as the rest—must seem like a genius. And it must appear an astonishing combination of genius with a whole series of extraordinary coincidences that this ram, instead of entering the common pen each evening, ends up in a special one where he gets extra oats, and that this particular ram, swelling with fat, is eventually killed for mutton.

But the sheep only need to stop assuming that everything happening to them is designed for their sheepish purposes; they only need to admit that what happens to them may serve purposes beyond their understanding—and they will immediately see a unity and coherence in what is being done to the fattened ram. Even if they don't know why he's being fattened, at least they'll know that everything that happens to the ram doesn't happen by accident, and they'll have no need for the concepts of "chance" or "genius."

Only by giving up our claim to understand some immediately obvious purpose, and accepting that the ultimate purpose is beyond our grasp, can we see the chain of experiences in the lives of historical figures and perceive the cause of the effect they produce, which is disproportionate to their ordinary human abilities. Only then will we have no need for the words "chance" and "genius."

We need only acknowledge that we do not know the purpose of the European upheavals, and that we only know the facts—that is, the killings, first in France, then in Italy, Africa, Prussia, Austria, Spain, and Russia—and that the movements from west to east and from east to west form the essential substance of those events. Only then will we no longer need to see something exceptional—some stroke of genius—in the characters of Napoleon and Alexander, and will no longer need to attribute the event to some individual's specific quality.

By abandoning any claim to knowledge of the ultimate purpose, we will clearly see that just as it's impossible to imagine a blossom or seed better suited to a plant than the one it actually produces, so too it's impossible to imagine any two people more perfectly adapted, down to the smallest detail, to fulfill the roles that Napoleon and Alexander played.
